variants.name: Typed generic fan-out joined by Promise.all / Promise.allSettled
variants.implementation_notes: TypeScript runs on the same single-threaded event loop as JavaScript, so the master is still Promise.all over async sub-tasks; the language's contribution is the contract. Model each sub-task as a generic Task<I, O> or as a discriminated union of request and response messages, so partition, dispatch and combine type-check and the master cannot mix partials from different sub-services. The runtime boundary is not typed - worker messages are structured-cloned and arrive as unknown - so narrow them with a type guard or schema at the boundary instead of casting. Choose Promise.all for fail-fast, allSettled when every partial matters (quorum or voting), bound the in-flight set, and remember that a rejection is a report, not a cancellation.
pitfalls: Casting (as Partial) on values that cross a worker or network boundary hides protocol drift; narrow with a type guard at the edge.
Promise.all rejects on the first failure while siblings keep running; allSettled keeps every partial but loses the failure reason unless each result is narrowed.
A CPU-bound sub-task blocks the event loop for all siblings - the typed contract does not make it parallel.
Unbounded fan-out over a large input holds every task and partial in memory; chunk the dispatch.

variants.name: Typed worker_threads pool with a request/response envelope (Node.js)
variants.implementation_notes: For CPU-bound sub-tasks the workers must be real threads: a fixed pool of node:worker_threads Workers with a generic run<TReq, TRes>(request): Promise<TRes> facade keeps the master's dispatch and combine typed while the pool owns worker reuse and correlation. The docs warn that a Worker per task costs more than the task and point at AsyncResource for correlating tasks in diagnostics. Payloads are structured-cloned or transferred, so type precisely which fields are copied and which are transferred (a transferred ArrayBuffer leaves the sender unusable); a crashed worker must be replaced by the pool and its in-flight promise settled, because exit codes and error events - not exceptions - signal failure.
pitfalls: Generics on the pool guarantee nothing about the runtime message shape: validate or narrow the worker's response before trusting the type.
Transferring an ArrayBuffer neuters the sender's view, and shared mutation needs SharedArrayBuffer plus Atomics - both break the independent-workers assumption.
Worker crash/exit is an event, not an exception: the pool must replace the worker and reject or requeue the in-flight job, or the master hangs on a promise that never settles.
Pool size must track cores; per-task Worker creation is the documented anti-pattern.
